claims.text: Anthropic's long-running agent harness for the Claude Agent SDK uses two parts: an initializer agent that sets up the environment on the first run, and a coding agent that makes incremental progress in every session while leaving clear artifacts for the next session.

The initializer agent's first session uses a specialized prompt to create an init.sh script, a claude-progress.txt file logging what agents have done, and an initial git commit showing which files were added.
Agents quickly understand the state of work when starting with a fresh context window through the claude-progress.txt file alongside the git history.

The initializer agent writes a comprehensive feature requirements file expanding on the user's prompt, with all features initially marked as "failing", to stop the agent from one-shotting the app or prematurely considering the project complete.

Coding agents are told to edit the feature list only by changing the status of a passes field, with strongly worded instructions such as "It is unacceptable to remove or edit tests because this could lead to missing or buggy functionality."
Anthropic used JSON for the feature list because the model is less likely to inappropriately change or overwrite JSON files than Markdown files.
Asking the coding agent to work on only one feature at a time was critical to addressing the agent's tendency to do too much at once.

To leave the environment clean, the model is asked to commit progress to git with descriptive commit messages and write progress summaries to a progress file, which lets it use git to revert bad changes and recover working states.

Each coding agent starts a session by running pwd, reading git logs and progress files, and reading the feature list to choose the highest-priority unfinished feature; it also runs a basic end-to-end test of the dev server (started via init.sh) before implementing a new feature.

Anthropic states it is still unclear whether a single general-purpose coding agent performs best or whether a multi-agent architecture with specialized agents (testing, quality assurance, code cleanup) would do better.

In the multi-agent research system, three factors explained 95% of performance variance on the BrowseComp evaluation, and token usage by itself explained 80% of the variance, with number of tool calls and model choice as the other two factors.

Agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats, so they require tasks valuable enough to pay for the increased performance.
Upgrading to Claude Sonnet 4 was a larger performance gain than doubling the token budget on Claude Sonnet 3.7.
The Research system uses an orchestrator-worker pattern in which a lead agent analyzes the query, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents that search different aspects in parallel.

Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on tools and sources, and clear task boundaries; without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information.

Because agents struggle to judge appropriate effort, scaling rules were embedded in prompts: simple fact-finding uses 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research more than 10 subagents.
Overinvestment in simple queries was a common failure mode in early versions of the Research system.
Parallelization, with the lead agent spinning up 3-5 subagents in parallel and subagents using 3+ tools in parallel, cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries.
Lead agents execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set to complete, which simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks in information flow.
Anthropic uses rainbow deployments, gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while both run, to avoid disrupting running agents.

For long conversations, agents summarize completed work phases and store essential information in external memory, and can spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts with careful handoffs when context limits approach.
Subagents can write outputs to a filesystem as artifacts, bypassing the lead coordinator, to minimize the 'game of telephone' and improve fidelity and performance.

The Claude Agent SDK supports subagents by default for parallelization and context management, since subagents use isolated context windows and send only relevant information back to the orchestrator.
The Claude Agent SDK's compact feature automatically summarizes previous messages when the context limit approaches, and is built on Claude Code's compact slash command.

SDK compaction replaces older messages with a summary, so specific instructions from early in the conversation may not be preserved; it emits a system message with subtype "compact_boundary", and /compact can be sent to trigger it manually.
